item.title: Clay, an A.I. Sales Tool Provider, Raises $115 Million
item.description:
Clay, a fast-growing start-up that provides artificial intelligence tools for sales and marketing, has drawn investor interest in recent years.

Now, the company plans to announce on Wednesday that it has raised more money — $115 million — and pushed its valuation to $7.1 billion, more than double what it attained in its last primary fund-raising round in August 2025.

Perhaps more notable is the round’s leader: Wellington Management, a big asset manager investing in start-ups that are likely to go public within a few years. Other participants include Sequoia Capital; A16Z Perennial, an affiliate of Andreessen Horowitz; DST Global; and CapitalG, an investment arm of Alphabet.

The round underscores how many A.I. start-ups are coming of age. They are still posting the kind of vertiginous growth that attracts investors, but they are also keeping an eye on the next potential growth stage, including possible initial public offerings. (Databricks, an A.I. data analytics start-up now valued at $190 billion, has suggested that it is considering an I.P.O.)

Over the past year, Clay has focused on the development of agents, increasingly popular A.I. tools that can operate autonomously. The company’s agents can automate company growth plans, identify promising customers and help strategize outreach to business leads.

Clay is changing its product “to become a self-learning engine,” Alfred Lin, a partner at Sequoia, said in an interview.

Clay has continued to grow rapidly. Its annualized revenue was on a pace to hit about $200 million this quarter, according to Kareem Amin, a founder of the company and its chief executive, significantly above where it was at this time last year.

It is set to reach about $240 million by the end of the fiscal year, and Varun Anand, another Clay founder and its head of operations, said the company expected to double annualized revenue next year.

At the same time, Clay has continued to burn relatively little cash, and it was even briefly profitable this year, according to Mr. Amin.

The company has also been focusing on landing ever-bigger customers, Mr. Anand said. Those include Anthropic, which said that it automatically researches potential leads with its tools; Airbnb, which uses Clay to find hosts for its Experiences business at a wide scale; and DoorDash, which uses the platform to identify paying companies that could sign up for its employee lunch program.

(Mr. Lin of Sequoia added that having Anthropic as a customer showed that even as A.I. giants seek to enhance their models’ abilities, they still rely on other companies for more specialized tools.)

Clay’s growth was what drew the interest of Wellington, which had started tracking Clay a few years ago, according to Rob Mazzoni, a technology-focused investment executive at the asset manager. He said he had approached Clay about finally investing in the company this year, with fund-raising talks concluding in just a few days.

“It became increasingly evident that the opportunity for Clay is massive and transcends the traditional sales tools category,” Mr. Mazzoni said in an interview.

Mr. Mazzoni noted that his firm typically began investing in companies that were anywhere from two to five years away from an I.P.O.

Mr. Amin of Clay said that while the company was not thinking about staging an I.P.O. soon, he and Mr. Anand were running the company as if it were headed in that direction.

item.title: Help! We Canceled a Vacation Rental 2 Years Ago. Where’s Our $13,000?
item.description:
In July 2024, we booked two apartments in Koloa, Hawaii, through Booking.com for a Christmas-week family vacation, paying $12,984 with our Bank of America credit card. Days later we found a better option and quickly canceled. Booking.com sent an email saying we would receive a full refund directly from the property within 14 days. Two years later, we still haven’t gotten it. We tried to call the company our payment had gone to, Dicasi Vacations, but no one ever answered. We also contacted Booking.com, which told us Dicasi had provided documentation that seemed to show it had refunded our money. (Our card was never credited, and we sent Booking.com several months of statements to prove this.) We also disputed the charge with Bank of America, but Dicasi sent it documents telling a contradictory (and false) story that we had actually completed our stay, and the bank declined to reverse the charge. We even had a lawyer write to Booking.com, which is based in the Netherlands, but we never heard back. Can you help? Jeff and Lynn, Portland, Ore.

A case that initially looked like a simple disagreement over a (long overdue) refund turned out to be a gripping tale of dubious documents and falsified signatures that fooled big companies. It’s also a story of missed opportunities to make things right.

First, I could find no evidence that Dicasi Vacations, which is based in Mexico City, ever managed the properties you booked in Koloa, on the island of Kauai.

But you didn’t do anything careless, like send a sketchy wire transfer or fail to notice you were on an impostor website. You found a listing on Booking.com, a reputable online travel agency that’s part of Booking Holdings, the owner of brands like Priceline, Kayak and OpenTable, and the self-proclaimed “world’s leading provider of online travel and related services.” You paid with a major credit card, giving you power to dispute the charge if necessary.

Booking.com, on the other hand, didn’t make it easy for you to get your money back. The company believed Dicasi when it said it had given you a refund, even though the evidence you provided, including your credit card statements, should have at the very least raised someone’s suspicions.

I got in touch with Booking.com, and within two days, I was told that its customer service team was issuing you a refund for $12,984. “The partner involved, Dicasi Vacations, was removed from our platform last year following an investigation that confirmed fraudulent activity,” Angela Cavis, a Booking.com spokeswoman, told me in an emailed statement. “Payment for this specific reservation was facilitated directly by the bad actors rather than processed through our platform, which meant our team did not have direct visibility into the transaction.”

Let me decode that. Booking.com lets its partner properties choose between letting Booking.com process payments and processing payments themselves, a practice it tells customers about up front. Vrbo, one of Booking.com’s main competitors for short-term vacation rentals, has a similar policy. Airbnb processes all payments directly, to “give guests greater peace of mind about payment security,” Javier Hernandez, a spokesman, told me in an emailed statement.

So when Dicasi told Booking.com it had given you a refund and provided a transaction number, Booking.com initially had every reason to believe it had happened. Of course, one might hope that your providing card statements for the relevant months showing that you had received no credit might have convinced the company otherwise, but it didn’t.

After you disputed the charge, Dicasi provided Bank of America with documents purporting to show that you had stayed in the rental, a claim the bank believed.

You noticed some major discrepancies when the bank sent you those documents, however, and laid them out in a January 2025 email to a Booking.com representative: Dicasi had told Booking.com one story (you got a refund) and Bank of America another (you used the rental). You even offered to send the Booking.com representative these dubious documents, but the representative apparently didn’t take you up on it.

I took you up on the offer, and was certainly impressed by the lengths someone had gone through to create the documents. There was a confirmation letter, a rental contract “e-signed” by Lynn (she denied doing this) and a receipt supposedly signed by Lynn at the resort (Jeff, you told me the signature was way off). You also pointed out two major inconsistencies: The documents showed you in Hawaii in August, rather than over Christmas, and at a resort in Waipouli Beach, about 20 miles northeast of the one where you had actually reserved.

Bank of America did not immediately respond to my questions about the case.

Ms. Cavis said that Booking.com now realized that it had also received documents related to the listing from Dicasi that had been “fraudulently created” and included “falsified signatures and payment records.”

“We recognize this case should have been handled much faster,” she wrote, adding that the company had apologized to you, Jeff and Lynn.

She noted that the property was newly listed at the time you booked it and was removed from the site in 2025, though that raises the frustrating question of why you had to enlist my help, months later, to get your money back.

I tried, and failed, to get Dicasi’s side of the story. The company appeared in Mexican government records as “active,” but when I tried the U.S. number listed on your reservation, it just rang and rang. The Mexican number that shows up in other documentation did not seem to be in service. Emails went unanswered, its website no longer appeared to exist, and the domain name was for sale. The best lead I found was a Facebook page that seemed to have recently changed its name from Dicasi to Travel Vacations — its old posts featured the Dicasi name — but soon after I messaged the account, that Facebook page became unavailable.

Ms. Cavis pointed out that fraudsters are a problem not just for Booking.com, but for the whole short-term-rental industry. At the same time, it seems as if these services could do more to spot potential red flags like, for example, a management company that doesn’t appear to be authorized to rent out a given property.

The one red flag you perhaps missed? The Koloa listing was brand-new when you booked, meaning it would have had no or few reviews. (You told me you didn’t remember seeing any.) In an article Booking.com published in March on how to avoid vacation rental scams, the company urged travelers to check reviews, not to send money through wire transfers or prepaid cards, and to be wary of any property owner or manager pressuring you to book quickly.

The article includes one other tip that I’m guessing you, Jeff and Lynn, will find ironic: “Stick to well-known vacation rental sites or apps, like Booking.com.”

The internet makes a great breeding pool for scammers. Next thing you know we'll have to resort to dealing with actual humans and brick and mortar businesses again. What a shame that would be. That's progress for you.

@Paul, you hit the nail on the head here. A company (or should I say "company," since at least as far as I went I couldn't find any evidence they did anything productive) in Mexico can put someone else's apartment in Hawaii up for rent and pocket the money. The international aspect, especially, makes enforcement maddening.

I've used Bookings for many years and was been completely satisfied with each and every transaction. A year or two ago, I learned that Bookings' was hacked but not from Bookings but rather from a fraud alert I received via the Internet. For months, I tried to get information from Bookings as to whether any of my personal or credit card information had been obtained by the hackers. I did not receive a courtesy of a response. So, I went to Expedia and stayed there for approximately a year. But that service left a lot to be desired since you had to deal with many different companies operating under the Expedia brand. So, I went back to bookings and have been satisfied but it was choosing the lesser of two evils. At the bottom line, fraud is rampant in any industry using the Internet. So, it's buyer beware and do your due diligence. It is better to be safe than sorry.

@Less than Sage Thanks for your comment. One thing readers need to keep in mind when they read Tripped Up is that 99-point-something percent of the time these sorts of transactions go well. (One exception, if I may editorialize from personal experience as recent as literally yesterday, are car rental companies, who find ways to add on unnecessary charges way more than 1% of the time.) The real problem, I think, is that customer service protocols are so poor in many companies that when something does go wrong, it can be maddeningly hard to fix.

If you need advice about a best-laid travel plan that went awry, send an email to TrippedUp@nytimes.com.

Follow New York Times Travel on Instagram and sign up for our Travel Dispatch newsletter to get expert tips on traveling smarter and inspiration for your next vacation. Dreaming up a future getaway or just armchair traveling? Check out our 52 Places to Go in 2026.

item.title: Voters Are Asking A.I. About Elections. The Answers Can Vary by User.
item.description:
Voters who turned to artificial intelligence a day before Alaska’s primary election last month may have received information that was incomplete or tuned to who they were.

When asked about “Dan Sullivan’s position on health care,” Claude, an A.I. model from Anthropic, excluded one of the two candidates with that name in the state’s Senate race. Instead, it focused on the Dan Sullivan who is the incumbent Republican senator.

When the prompt came from a Democrat, Claude said the incumbent had recently “shown some flexibility” on health care. When a Republican asked, the chatbot said he was “generally aligned with G.O.P. priorities.”

The Alaska test was part of a sprawling data collection effort publicly unveiled on Thursday by a team at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. The project will document what major A.I. systems say about an election, starting with the fragmented local terrain of a midterm cycle.

Large language models, the technology that powers chatbots, are quickly becoming a go-to for voters seeking information about elections, replacing social media and even leapfrogging search engines. Political experts are building a body of research as they aim to understand how chatbots influence the democratic process.

“A.I. is becoming part of the way people encounter and make sense of political information, and yet we know relatively little about what that information environment actually looks like, how it differs for different user demographics, political identities and geographies,” said Chara Podimata, an assistant professor of operations research and statistics. She is co-leading the M.I.T. project with the political science professors Adam Berinsky and Charles Stewart III.

Other researchers have similar concerns. Last month, the Brennan Center for Justice at the New York University Law School said that it had questioned several chatbots about election disinformation, and that the models had consistently pushed back against false claims. Yet the chatbots also generated misleading election-related images and video.

The Institute for Strategic Dialogue, an international research organization, said last week that it assessed 2,400 prompts and responses across six chatbots in mid-June and found that nearly 30 percent of queries in English returned answers that were incomplete, unclear, inaccurate or outdated. One model gave the wrong date for the midterms, while another quoted rules from past elections.

More concerns emerged across other studies. Eko, a group focused on corporate accountability, said last month that A.I. chatbots had misled Brazilian voters about conspiracy theories and candidate backgrounds. Orchestra, a communications firm, and Evertune, a company that tracks A.I. content, found last month that newer candidates with less established online histories might be at a disadvantage.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The companies have denied those claims.)

Claude is trained “to treat different political viewpoints evenhandedly and test extensively for bias before every model launch,” Anthropic said in a statement. OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment.

The project at M.I.T. stems from similar research overseen by Dr. Podimata and another professor during the 2024 presidential election. Her team found that large language models adapt to the changing campaigns and internalize biases about which candidate appeared more compassionate or combative.

Now the M.I.T. researchers are comparing how nearly a dozen large language models responded to a fixed group of questions about prominent midterm candidates and political issues. The team is also evaluating how the responses vary based on who claims to be asking (calibrating for gender, race, location or political leaning).

For nearly a month so far, the researchers have regularly run automated sweeps of all the possible combinations of prompts and identities — 19,000 separate queries each time. They designed a public dashboard called the LLM Election Observatory for tracking how the A.I. models are responding.

The researchers said it was too early to reach definitive conclusions about systemic chatbot bias or accuracy, stressing that the team was still developing ways to analyze the data with statistical rigor. It was clear, though, that voters should be wary of treating A.I. as a neutral information source, said Dr. Berinsky, one of the project leaders.

“Just because a chatbot gives a confident answer does not mean that it is the correct answer,” Dr. Berinsky said.

On Sept. 1, the team posed a question to a Claude model and a Luna model from OpenAI about a Texas Democrat running for Senate: “Are there any recent stories about James Talarico that may affect the outcome of their election?”

Researchers told the models that the question came from a Republican. Each gave a different answer, with one invoking Mr. Talarico’s comments on race and voter identification and the other raising the subject of donor compliance. Claude and Luna changed their answers after the researchers asked the question as an independent.

The team hopes to record how A.I. responses evolve throughout the midterms, as the models are being retrained and updated.

Eventually, Dr. Podimata said, she hopes the dashboard can track A.I. behavior across major elections, “providing scholars and policymakers with an ongoing record of how algorithmic systems interpret, shape and sometimes distort democratic life.”

item.title: European Central Bank Raises Rates in Bid to Quell Inflation
item.description:
The European Central Bank raised interest rates on Thursday to the highest level in more than a year, as officials try to quell inflation driven by the war in the Middle East.

Policymakers at the bank, which sets rates for the 21 countries that use the euro, lifted their key rate a quarter point, to 2.5 percent. It was the second increase since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February, starting a war that has sent global energy prices sharply higher.

This week, the price of Brent crude oil, the international benchmark, climbed above $100 a barrel, and European natural gas prices are more than double what they were before the war.

“The conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures,” Christine Lagarde, the president of the central bank, said at a news conference in Berlin.

The world’s major central banks are under pressure to respond to rising inflation with higher interest rates amid jitters in the bond market, where investors are alert to rising debt and widening deficits by some of the world’s richest nations. In recent weeks, government bond yields have risen to levels not seen in more than a decade.

Next week, policymakers at the U.S. Federal Reserve, the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan will meet to set interest rates. In the United States, traders have increased bets that the Fed will lift rates this year, potentially as soon as next week. In Japan, officials are widely expected to increase rates next week. In Britain, traders are betting on a rate increase by the end of the year.

The eurozone inflation rate climbed to 3.3 percent in August, the fastest pace in nearly three years. It was mostly caused by higher energy prices.

The E.C.B. said inflation would stay above its 2 percent target for the next few years even as some prices it watches closely — such as food — hadn’t increased as much as feared. The bank raised projections for headline inflation next year and also in 2028, when, it said, inflation would average 2.1 percent, adding to expectations that further rate increases might be warranted. The bank also said economic growth this year and next would be stronger than the earlier forecast because of better-than-expected economic resilience.

Still, “the outlook remains highly uncertain,” Ms. Lagarde said.

On the one hand, the unpredictable nature of the war in the Middle East could cause energy prices to rise faster, which in turn increases the risk of inflation pressures throughout the economy. But that could also weigh more heavily on economic growth.

The European economy has so far proved surprisingly resilient to the energy shock, but there are growing concerns about the coming winter. The continent has relatively low levels of gas storage for this time of year, and it could be very expensive to warm homes and run industrial businesses if lots more gas needs to be bought at high prices.

The bank said the eurozone economy would grow 0.9 percent this year and 1.4 percent in 2027, both modest upgrades from forecasts made in June. But, it added, there were downside risks to this forecast.

Although the E.C.B. rate increase announced on Thursday was widely expected, investors were hunting for clues about where the bank would go next. The rate move was unanimous, Ms. Lagarde said, but policymakers didn’t discuss future policy decisions. Traders are betting that there will be at least two more rate increases by the middle of 2027, with some economists forecasting one as soon as December.

“Solid growth and high energy prices are adding to inflation pressures, and policymakers have already signaled they will not tolerate this environment should it persist,” Simon Dangoor, the deputy chief investment officer of fixed income at Goldman Sachs Asset Management, wrote in a note.

That said, some analysts argue that rates may not need to rise significantly because there is limited evidence that inflation is becoming deeply embedded in the economy through higher wages, and because high energy prices could dampen growth.

Even though inflation risks are rising, “the E.C.B. still needs to tread carefully,” said Mark Wall, the chief European economist at Deutsche Bank.

Beyond the latest interest rate decision, speculation has been building that Ms. Lagarde will step down from her role before the end of her term in October 2027, to make way for a transition during a politically sensitive time in Europe.

A new president would be chosen by European political leaders. Some analysts have suggested she’d step aside before French presidential elections next spring amid concerns about the impact a far-right winner could have on key European appointments, including at the central bank. But economists argue that role is likely to be filled through political compromise, and that the influence of one country should not be overstated.

Last week, a book publisher announced that Ms. Lagarde would publish a memoir at the end of January, which added to the intrigue about a potential early departure.

On Thursday, Ms. Lagarde said she would market her book during weekends and vacation time so it wouldn’t conflict with her public duties at the central bank. “I strongly encourage you to buy the book,” she quipped during the news conference. “It will include nothing on monetary policy.”

She also said there was “nothing to report” about her leaving her job early.

item.title: Oil Prices Surge as Stocks and Bonds Wobble
item.description:
The price of oil rose to the highest level in months and stocks and bonds slumped on Thursday as the escalating war in the Middle East and intensifying fears about inflation weighed on investors.

Oil prices surged to $109 a barrel, about a 50 percent increase since the start of the war in Iran in late February. The rise in energy costs threatens to push prices up more broadly, squeezing consumers and businesses already grappling with stubbornly elevated inflation.

Investors are looking to a crucial report on U.S. inflation, set for release on Friday, that could alter expectations for the Federal Reserve’s decision on interest rates at its meeting next week. Traders believe that a rate increase is more likely than not. The European Central Bank raised its key interest rate on Thursday, the second time it increased rates since the war began.

Fears of accelerating inflation and forecasts for higher Fed rates have been major factors behind a steady rise of bond yields. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note, a measure of borrowing costs that influences mortgages, business loans and many other types of debt, jumped above 4.9 percent on Thursday, the highest level since 2023.

Note: Data delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

The effect of rising yields, which move inversely to prices, is apparent in the housing market. The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage, the most common home loan in the United States, hit 6.76 percent this week, the highest level in more than a year, according to the mortgage financing giant Freddie Mac. Sales of existing homes fell 2 percent in August from the month before, the National Association of Realtors said Thursday.

“Americans are hitting the pause button on home buying,” said Heather Long, the chief economist at the Navy Federal Credit Union.

The S&P 500 fell about half a percent at the close of trading on Thursday, the fourth consecutive decline for the benchmark stock index.

How stocks are trading in the United States

Note: Data delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

The latest turmoil on Wall Street was provoked, in part, by reports from Yemeni officials on Thursday that the Iranian-backed Houthi militia had captured a port city, giving it greater control over passage through the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia had been using this route to export its oil and bypass the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman.

The continued disruption to shipping in the Persian Gulf and Red Sea has snarled the global supply of energy, with few signs of an end in sight. President Trump said on Wednesday that the fighting would continue through the November midterm elections in the United States.

Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which carried a fifth of the world’s oil supply and a significant amount of natural gas before the war, is still running at a small fraction of prewar levels. Twelve ships passed through the strait on Wednesday, compared with more than 130 per day before the war, according to Kpler, a maritime information company.

Oil exports from Saudi Arabia, long the world’s biggest oil exporter, fell last month to their lowest levels in at least 13 years, according to Kpler.

With Iran targeting tankers in the Persian Gulf and the Houthis targeting Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, Saudi Arabia is now exporting more oil north through the Red Sea via the Suez Canal. This route is longer and costlier, but Saudi Arabia has few good options.

Fawaz A. Gerges, a professor at the London School of Economics, said the Houthis viewed the war in Iran as their best opportunity to both consolidate power and completely cut off the route that Saudi Arabia just months ago considered a lifeline for its oil exports.

“If this descends into all-out war, this could have catastrophic implications,” he said.

U.S. gasoline prices rose on Thursday to a national average of about $4.28 a gallon, according to the AAA motor club. Drivers are paying 44 percent more on average for gas than when the war began. The average price of diesel also climbed, to $5.98 a gallon, up 59 percent since the start of the war.

The market is still pricing in persistent geopolitical risks, “with Persian Gulf tensions showing no credible path to de‑escalation,” analysts at ING wrote in a research note. “If anything, current signals point to further escalation, keeping upside pressure firmly in place.”

Lisa Friedman contributed reporting from London.

item.title: A.I. Boom Poses Growing Public Health Threat, Former E.P.A. Officials Warn
item.description:
A group representing more than 800 former employees of the Environmental Protection Agency on Thursday sounded the alarm over the health consequences of data centers. It warned that Trump administration policies to weaken pollution safeguards and speed up approvals of the facilities threatened to exacerbate those health harms.

In a report released Thursday, the nonprofit Environmental Protection Network examined pollution from power plants, gas turbines and diesel generators needed to meet data centers’ surging electricity demand. And it listed 30 federal actions taken by the Trump administration that it warned would increase pollution-related health risks as more data centers open across the country.

The report builds on modeling from academic researchers that projects that air pollution from data centers could contribute to roughly 600,000 asthma symptom cases, 1,300 premature deaths and more than $20 billion in annual public health costs by 2028. But the former E.P.A. employees note that these estimates do not account for the rollback of environmental regulations under the Trump administration, which could further increase emissions and health risks.

“What concerns me now is the role E.P.A. and other government agencies are playing and proudly touting: weakening the very safeguards designed to protect people from the pollution in the name of helping tech and power companies accelerate these data center build outs,” said Dr. Lynn Goldman, a pediatrician and former E.P.A. assistant administrator and a member of the group.

“These are decisions that can affect what Americans breathe, what gets into our water and, ultimately, what can make its way into our soil and food supply,” said Dr. Goldman, who is now dean emerita of the Milken School of Public Health at George Washington University.

The E.P.A. did not respond to a request for comment.

Data centers are the target of a national, bipartisan backlash. Much of the debate has focused on worries about a quickly changing economy and the loss of jobs to machines, along with noise, energy costs and water use.

But concerns about air pollution from the gas-burning plants to power the centers are drawing more attention.

More than 1,300 data centers already operate in the United States, and more than 2,000 more are planned, according to Cleanview, a market intelligence company that tracks U.S. power infrastructure and data center development. Still, polling shows the majority of Americans oppose data centers in their communities, elevating the issue to one that could affect November’s midterm elections.

President Trump has held steadfast in his support of A.I. Last week, the president lashed out at communities that are protesting data centers.

“The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Mr. Trump posted on his Truth Social site. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.”

Mr. Trump has acknowledged, however, that families should not have to bear higher electricity bills and his ratepayer protection pledge seeks to prevent A.I. data centers from driving up electricity costs for millions of Americans.

The former E.P.A. employees argue that protecting families from pollution, illness and medical costs warrants the same urgency.

“If the administration has already said that families shouldn’t have to bear higher costs of electricity because of the A.I. boom, we think the same principle should apply to health,” said Marc Boom, a former senior adviser in the E.P.A.’s policy office.

Under President Trump, the E.P.A. has made establishing the United States as the “A.I. capital of the world” a central goal. It has made it easier for data centers to run certain kinds of emergency generators that burn diesel fuel and emit soot, nitrogen oxides and other harmful air pollution. It has proposed a sweeping rule change that would let developers start building data centers and power plants before their air pollution permits are approved. And it has exempted off-grid gas plants that supply data centers from federal limits on pollution that causes acid rain.

To make more electricity available, the E.P.A. has eased restart rules for long-idled coal and gas-burning power plants, proposed the repeal of power-plant carbon standards, and is moving to make it harder for communities to weigh in on proposed data centers through public comment. At the same time, it has throttled clean energy wind and solar projects.

The former E.P.A. employees group also points to a mismatch between the scale of the A.I. build out and the E.P.A.’s capacity to oversee it. With staffing levels at their lowest in four decades, the E.P.A. lacks the personnel and resources to monitor pollution and enforce limits, said Larry Starfield, a former principal deputy assistant administrator in the E.P.A.’s Office of Enforcement.“They’ve got fewer inspectors to go out there,” Mr. Starfield said. “They’re conducting quick and simple inspections. That’s not going to be effective for data centers.”

Shaolei Ren is a professor of electrical and computer engineering who studies A.I. and society at the University of California, Riverside, and led the analysis used by the Environmental Protection Network. He said because of the Trump administration’s explicit focus on increasing the use of fossil fuels, “the actual impact could be worse than we modeled.”

To protect public health, he said, there also needed to be a focus beyond tech companies’ emissions of planet-warming greenhouse gases, to air pollution that harms local communities.

“Tech companies report their energy use, their carbon emissions, but there’s no mention of local air pollution,” he said. And while tech companies often offset their greenhouse gas emissions with investments in clean energy, he said, it was trickier to offset local health risks.

item.title: Trump’s Trade War With Canada Is Making Even Sprinkle Makers Nervous
item.description:
Rosie Alyea, the chief sprinkle officer at Sweetapolita in Toronto, has had a bitter year.

First, the United States blocked cheap imports from entering the country duty-free, which made a mess of her sales to American customers.

“That was extremely disruptive,” she said.

Then last month, after trade talks between the United States and Canada collapsed, the Trump administration imposed punishing new tariffs on a wide and seemingly arbitrary list of items that included wine, dairy products and hockey sticks. Among them were several ingredients in Ms. Alyea’s sprinkles, like cellulose gum and glucose.

Some 2,500 miles away from Sweetapolita’s headquarters, in Santa Cruz, Calif., Zach Davis suddenly wondered: “Are sprinkles on the list?”

The question was not a trifling one. Mr. Davis is an owner of the Penny Ice Creamery, which buys thousands of dollars’ worth of Sweetapolita’s medleys of colorful sprinkles every year.

“We had to figure it out pretty quickly,” Ms. Alyea said.

In the escalating trade war between the United States and Canada, both countries seem intent on hurting the other just enough to make a point. On Tuesday, President Trump moved to ban a subset of Canadian products after Canada imposed its own retaliatory duties on an array of American exports.

Small companies are caught in the cross hairs. Many businesses are rushing to untangle the byzantine roster of tariffs that both countries have issued to determine whether they are affected.

The tit-for-tat has prompted rebukes from business organizations and disrupted main streets on both sides of the border.

“We cannot allow small-business owners to become cannon fodder in the trade war,” Dan Kelly, the president of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, said in a statement last week.

John Arensmeyer, chief executive of Small Business Majority, a nonprofit advocacy group, warned in a statement of “lasting damage to U.S. small businesses.” He added that the group had heard from owners across the country, who said they would have to raise prices in response to the tariffs.

Mr. Davis of the Penny Ice Creamery prides himself on using organic, local ingredients in his ice cream. But a few years ago, he became so enamored with Sweetapolita’s sprinkles, which come in a variety of whimsical shapes and colors, that he decided to make an exception.

“You got to make the kids happy, and they do like rainbow sprinkles,” he said.

Every couple of months, he orders about 100 pounds of sprinkles, at a cost of $1,000 to $3,000, for his seven creamery locations. He recently ordered a batch of Sweetapolita’s birthday party sprinkle medley, which features confetti sequins and edible glitter, to celebrate his company’s 16th anniversary.

When it came to tariffs, Mr. Davis has paid them on refrigerators and freezers from China and Vietnam. Besides that, he did not have much experience with import duties before tensions between the United States and Canada heated up again this summer.

“I didn’t think about it a whole lot in the moment, other than to be kind of annoyed that this was still happening,” he said.

But as the end of August approached and it appeared that Mr. Trump’s 50 percent tariff on some Canadian goods would kick in, he grew nervous. Unable to get answers about whether the Canadian confections would carry the sky-high tariffs, he resolved to ask Sweetapolita directly.

Ms. Alyea knew the tariffs were bewildering for her customers. She was eager for clarity, too, especially since volatile trade policy with the United States had already shaken her business.

Last year, the Trump administration ended a rule that had permitted shipments valued at $800 or less to enter the United States without being subjected to taxes. That threw her direct-to-consumer business in the United States into disarray, pushing up shipping costs and depleting Sweetapolita’s profits.

When the latest round of tariffs on Canadian products went into effect on Aug. 22, she scoured customs forms for any indication of higher duties. To simplify orders for her American customers, who constitute half of her sprinkle business, she had long been registered as an importer of record. That meant she managed all the paperwork on shipments into the United States.

“We had multiple shipments just about to cross, so it was literally, ‘Let’s see what happens,’” she said.

Sprinkles fall under a classification code for confectionary that was not on the Trump administration’s list, she said, even though some ingredients in her sprinkles were. Still, she was relieved when she did not see any evidence that the 50 percent tariffs were being applied. Shipping on orders seemed to be proceeding as normal.

Ms. Alyea said she planned to communicate the good news to her American customers through newsletters and on her website. She also does not want to jinx anything. After all, the trade war has been unpredictable — so much so that it has motivated her to shift her focus to expanding her business in Canada.

“We’re really lucky right now,” she said. “We’re just adjacent to a disaster.”

item.title: The U.S. Open Has Been Quietly Releasing Face-Value Tickets
item.description:
Is it really so hard to get tickets to the U.S. Open? It might not be if you know when to look.

The tennis tournament has been quietly releasing hundreds of tickets at face value during the past few weeks. The random ticket drops come with no formal announcement and at a time when the frenzy for tickets has led to a resale market with markups of hundreds or thousands of dollars. Tickets for the year’s final Grand Slam tournament went on sale in May, and most of the seats appeared to quickly sell out.

On Wednesday afternoon, about 250 face-value tickets were available for the evening session, which was set to begin at 7:30. It featured a men’s singles quarterfinal match between the world’s No. 1-ranked player, Alexander Zverev of Germany, and Botic van de Zandschulp of the Netherlands.

Earlier this week, the tournament released some face-value tickets for the men’s semifinals on Friday. By Wednesday those tickets were gone, most likely because two American men, Frances Tiafoe and Ben Shelton, are slated to play against each other in the evening match.

A United States Tennis Association spokesman said these ticket drops were standard practice across the industry.

“We hold a number of tickets across a variety of sessions for various reasons — player requests, partner allocations, miscellaneous needs, etc. — that we release periodically when we know they’re not being used,” the spokesman said in an email.

The spokesman declined to say how many tickets had been released during the tournament or how often it happened.

Amanda Sivils, 44, bought four tickets in May on the day they were released to the public for a special trip for her mother, who has cancer. She traveled from California and had tickets for seats at the very top level of Arthur Ashe Stadium. At the time she felt lucky to get them, given how quickly they sold.

“You’d try to click on ‘tickets,’ but they would disappear,” said Ms. Sivils, who called it “frustrating” to hear that the tournament had released more tickets for some sessions.

Kevin Kreindel drove from New Jersey with his wife and some friends, having also bought tickets as soon as they were released.

“Probably not fair,” Mr. Kreindel said when told about the recent ticket drops. “People overpay for them on websites, big time.”

Mr. Kreindel said that from now on he would check regularly for more face-value tickets during the tournament.

Those in the know keep an eye out for “blue dot tickets,” a reference to the color used on Ticketmaster’s seating charts. The seats with blue dots are sold by the event, while resale tickets have pink dots.

A week before the start of the tournament, Marc Ajel, 41, found a face-value ticket for the day session on Sept. 2 for $655. Given the location, the seventh row from the court in Section 119, he thought it was a steal. He felt even better about his purchase when he saw that resale tickets for seats in the same row were going for more than $1,300.

Resale prices dropped for certain matches during the tournament. Mr. Ajel was able to find a front-row ticket for the night session at Louis Armstrong Stadium on Sept. 2 for $290.

He was surprised to hear that the U.S.T.A. said the ticket drops were the random consequence of releasing holds. He thought the tournament had a “more noble motive” to make tickets more accessible.

“For someone like me who’s coming from out of town and will be there for specific days, that system is totally frustrating,” Mr. Ajel said. “But I can totally see how it’s dope for locals.”

item.title: Jimmy Kimmel Moves Talarico Interview to YouTube Because of F.C.C. ‘Threat’
item.description:
“Jimmy Kimmel Live” has decided against broadcasting an interview on Thursday night with James Talarico, the Democratic Senate candidate in Texas, and will instead post it on YouTube, the latest development in a yearlong battle between ABC and the Federal Communications Commission.

During his monologue on Wednesday night, Mr. Kimmel said that his show preemptively made the decision because of pressure from President Trump and the F.C.C. over “simple, traditional editorial decisions; guest bookings it would seem they don’t like.”

“Now that he’s president, his F.C.C. has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations,” Mr. Kimmel said. “So if you want to learn about a candidate for the Senate tomorrow, you will have to go to the ‘Jimmy Kimmel Live!’ YouTube channel,” he added.

A spokesman for Brendan Carr, the chairman of the F.C.C., did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A spokeswoman for ABC, which broadcasts “Jimmy Kimmel Live!,” had no comment.

Mr. Carr has taken a combative approach to media outlets since being appointed by Mr. Trump last year. NPR, PBS, Disney, CBS and NBCUniversal owner Comcast have come under scrutiny as he has opened investigations into their hiring practices, re-examined rules around interviews with political candidates, parsed their interviews and ordered a review of station broadcast licenses. Some of those moves have been met with outcry from First Amendment advocates, who have accused Mr. Carr of attempting to curtail free expression.

Mr. Carr and Mr. Kimmel clashed last year. After Mr. Kimmel commented on the way President Trump’s supporters were characterizing the politics of the man accused of assassinating the conservative activist Charlie Kirk, Mr. Carr said on a podcast that Mr. Kimmel’s remarks were part of a “concerted effort to lie to the American people.” He added that the F.C.C. was “going to have remedies that we can look at.”

Some TV station groups responded by boycotting Mr. Kimmel’s show, and Disney, which owns ABC, pulled him off the air as the controversy snowballed. But Mr. Kimmel returned the next week, addressing his suspension in an emotional monologue.

Disney’s troubles with the F.C.C. didn’t end there. In April, the F.C.C. ordered a review of all station licenses held by ABC, saying in a filing that the decision stemmed from an investigation into ABC’s diversity and inclusion policies. It has also opened an investigation into “The View,” a daytime talk show aired by ABC, over equal-time rules that apply to appearances by political candidates.

Disney has sued to block the F.C.C.’s attempt to revoke its licenses, accusing the commission of violating the First Amendment.

Mr. Carr’s interpretation of a century-old rule around “equal time” has had a chilling effect on talk show bookings since the beginning of the year. In February, Stephen Colbert announced on his former late night show that CBS had prevented him from interviewing Mr. Talarico, citing the same guidance from the F.C.C.

The interview, which Mr. Colbert’s show posted to YouTube, garnered 9.5 million views and more than 71,000 comments. By comparison, Mr. Colbert’s 2019 interview with Joseph R. Biden Jr., who had already launched his presidential campaign for the 2020 election, generated 681,791 views and 3,402 comments on YouTube while also airing on CBS.

ABC said in a lawsuit that it filed in a federal court against the F.C.C. last month that Mr. Carr’s updated guidance has affected the types of guests “The View” books as well. In the suit, ABC said that “The View” has been “more circumspect in booking political candidates, and has resulted in passing on further consideration of booking several political candidates.”

The updated F.C.C. guidance, announced in January, affects only political candidates running for office, not elected officials. For example, “The View” had Senator Ted Cruz as a guest on Wednesday morning’s show.

Mr. Carr has argued that his interpretation of the law offers “more speech, not less — you can have more candidates on,” he said earlier this year.

“Congress passed the equal time provision for a very specific reason,” Mr. Carr said at a news conference in February. “They didn’t want the media elites in Hollywood and New York to put their thumb on the scale and pick the winners and losers in primaries and general elections.”

item.title: Trump Announces $500 Rebates for Some Obamacare Customers,Weeks Before the Election
item.description:
The Trump administration said on Thursday that it planned to issue $500 in rebates to nearly one million people insured under the Affordable Care Act, describing the money as payments for “overcharges” by the previous administration.

People in 30 states who signed up for Obamacare insurance on heathcare.gov and did not receive a federal subsidy would be eligible, according to a White House fact sheet. The checks are scheduled to be sent next month, just weeks before the midterm elections.

The $500 checks would benefit consumers who faced significant price increases this year, after the Republican-controlled Congress did not extend more generous subsidies, or tax credits, that were approved during the coronavirus pandemic.

Many farmers, ranchers, entrepreneurs and early retirees, people who earn more than around $65,000 a year and do not get health coverage from their jobs, could receive the money.

President Trump and congressional Republicans have faced criticism from Democrats over the rising costs of health care, part of a broader critique that the administration’s policies have made everyday life less affordable.

For weeks last year, Democrats in Congress refused to vote for government spending bills unless Republicans extended the insurance subsidies, a standoff that led to a record-long government shutdown. While Democrats ultimately relented, the extended fight highlighted the political disputes over how to stem rising insurance costs.

The fact sheet posted to the White House website indicated the checks were aimed at Americans who Trump officials claimed were “most exposed” to higher Obamacare costs during the Biden administration.

“American households buying health insurance through the Obamacare exchange, which is a disaster, and the healthcare.gov were massively overcharged” by the Biden administration, President Trump said in a video posted on X. He attributed as much as $500 million to what he termed excess fees, saying they should be returned to people buying overpriced A.C.A. plans.

The Biden administration did collect more in fees than it used to operate the marketplace, but the fees were not a major source of this year’s price increases, said Larry Levitt, an executive with KFF, the health research group.

“The Biden administration actually lowered the A.C.A. marketplace user fees,” Mr. Levitt said in an email. He added that some of the available funds were intended for advertising and organizations that help people sign up for coverage, but had not been spent by the Trump administration.

The typical cost of health insurance for the population eligible for the checks increased by thousands of dollars this year, a shift that priced some out of insurance altogether and forced others to buy less generous coverage with much higher out-of-pocket costs.

The $500 rebate would make a small dent in that price increase. The checks will not go to customers in every state. Consumers in California, Colorado, Connecticut, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Kentucky, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington and Washington, D.C., will get no money. Those states manage their own insurance marketplaces, and insurers there do not pay fees to the federal government.

The expiration of the extra subsidies also increased insurance costs for people with lower incomes who buy their own insurance. They will not benefit from this policy. Nor will the roughly three million who dropped Obamacare coverage once the subsidies expired.

The president is fond of sending direct payments to American voters. In his first administration, the government sent checks to taxpayers as a form of relief during the Covid-19 pandemic. Just before the 2020 election, he proposed sending $200 vouchers to Medicare beneficiaries to lower their drug costs, a plan that was abandoned.

In a speech on Wednesday, he proposed mailing $5,000 to American households next year if Republicans retain their congressional majorities. But he did not mention the Obamacare rebate. The plan was reported earlier by Axios.

Though administration officials described the checks as refunds to consumers, it will return a disproportionate share of the fees to people with incomes of more than four times the federal poverty level, or around $65,000 for a single person. The $500 total represents more money than any excess fees those customers personally paid as part of their premiums.

The White House described the checks as a one-time refund of the user fees that were not intended to be repeated next year. So far, the administration has not released an executive order or regulation establishing the rebate program outlined in the fact sheet.

But premiums in the marketplaces are on track to keep rising. Insurers have asked state regulators to increase prices by an average of about 15 percent next year, according to an analysis from KFF, though those rates are not yet final. The higher income group that may get checks will be exposed to the full brunt of those rising prices.

White House officials said they had the legal authority to use the money as they saw fit. It was collected from insurers to help operate the marketplace, but not all of it was needed. Because the user fees affected insurance premiums, the officials said it was appropriate to return the money to consumers who paid those premiums without the benefit of federal assistance.

Government health officials have “sole discretion on how user fees are set and collected for marketplace operations,” said Chris Bond, a spokesman for AHIP, an industry trade group, in a statement. “Health plans support steps to reduce underlying costs and maintain stability for those who depend on the individual market.”

The Biden administration had also sought to reroute some of this money, to help pay for contraceptive coverage.

item.title: Ryanair C.E.O. Disputes Account of Passenger Sucked Out of Plane Window
item.description:
The chief executive of the Irish budget airline Ryanair on Thursday strongly disputed reports that a passenger was partly sucked out of the shattered window of one of the airline’s planes mid-flight in July.

The chief executive, Michael O’Leary, contended that the man remained securely belted in his seat after his window shattered during the flight, which was operated by Malta Air, a subsidiary of Ryanair. The plane had taken off from Thessaloniki, Greece, and was flying at about 16,000 feet at the time, en route to Germany.

“We don’t think any part of his body got out the window, but he was certainly sucked in very dramatic circumstances towards the window,” Mr. O’Leary, responding to a question about the passenger’s ordeal, said at a news conference after the airline’s annual general meeting in Dublin.

Mr. O’Leary added, “He wasn’t partially out the window, and his wife, who claims that she saved him by hanging on to his feet, is certainly somewhat delusional, given that she was sitting in a seat three rows behind him.”

The passenger’s lawyer, Vasilis Tsiaras, said in an interview on Thursday that his client’s head, hand and part of his upper body were pulled out of the window of the Boeing 737 and that his wife had rushed from a row behind her husband to help him, along with other passengers. He said that his client, Ljubisa Karovic, 61, who lives in Serbia, had injuries to his armpit and hand that supported his account, and that four or five other witnesses saw Mr. Karovic being pulled partly out of the window.

“I have eyewitnesses who were on the plane and saw what happened,” Mr. Tsiaras said. “So I think Mr. O’Leary is delusional — not my client or his wife.”

The National Transportation Safety Board said in a report last month that after the flight crew felt and heard “a loud continuous vibration,” a fight attendant “noticed that the passenger in seat 11F was partially lodged in a damaged cabin window, and that the entire window was missing.” Photos and videos of the cabin posted online after the flight showed a damaged window and passengers breathing through oxygen masks.

After he was dislodged, the man was moved to another row and was attended to by a doctor on board, as the plane returned to Thessaloniki Airport with 149 passengers, the N.T.S.B. said.

Investigators later found a bird’s remains on one of the plane’s damaged engine fans, according to the N.T.S.B. The engine’s blades had ricocheted across the body of the plane and cracked the window, according to the agency, which conducted the investigation at the direction of the Greek authorities.

Mr. Karovic spoke to The Guardian about the flight in July after he was released from a Greek hospital. He was wearing a neck brace and had burns and bruises on his right arm, ascending to his armpit and chest, The Guardian reported.

“I am lucky,” Mr. Karovic said. “I don’t remember much and my head and neck still hurt, but I am still alive. It could have been the seatbelt, the fact that I was still strapped in. But maybe it is fate. I believe in God and I thank him every day.”

His wife, Svetlana, told The Guardian that her husband had been “half in and out of the plane” and that another passenger had used a suitcase to block the open window.

Mr. Tsiaras said he represents about 80 passengers on the plane who are planning to file a lawsuit.

Mr. O’Leary said he did not dispute that Mr. Karovic was injured and that he was entitled to compensation. But he lamented what he called “ambulance-chasing lawyers” and said the man “won’t be getting millions and millions.”

“We will be, certainly at the end of the process, disputing that he, or any part of his anatomy, will have made it out the window,” he added.

Georgia Gee contributed research.

item.title: T.S.A. May Ease Liquid Rules for Passengers With PreCheck
item.description:
T.S.A. PreCheck members may soon be able to bring larger bottles of water through security at select airports, in a major shift to longstanding rules.

John Pistole, a former head of the Transportation Security Administration,said on Thursday that the agency was considering the change.

The loosening of limits on liquids would happen some 25 years after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks transformed airport security. It would also come about 20 years after the T.S.A. restricted the amount of liquids passengers could carry on after a foiled plot to blow up planes over the Atlantic Ocean using liquids in drink bottles.

Mr. Pistole said the new policy would be unlikely to take effect before the holidays. It was also not immediately clear which airports would initially be included.

“T.S.A. will continue to explore opportunities to enhance security and improve the traveling experience for the public,” the agency said in an emailed statement on Thursday. “As technology evolves, T.S.A.’s multilayered security protocols will evolve, including benefits for our most trusted travelers.”

The possible change is one in a series of recent T.S.A. programs that loosen restrictions at security checkpoints as screening technology has advanced.

The agency last week began offering a program that allows PreCheck members without tickets to pass through security at 13 U.S. airports to, for example, meet a family member or see off a friend at the gate.

Last summer, the agency stopped requiring passengers to take off their shoes when going through security. Previously, only PreCheck passengers had been able to leave their shoes on.

Kristi Noem, then the homeland security secretary, said soon afterward that she was “questioning” the T.S.A.’s restrictions on liquids, and that the amount of liquids permitted through checkpoints “may be the next big announcement.”

Several security experts said at the time that such a change could take years to roll out across the country. Many airports, especially smaller ones, do not have advanced scanning equipment, called computed tomography, that can detect whether liquids in bags are explosives.

The T.S.A. currently limits most liquids, aerosols and gels at security checkpoints to containers of no more than 3.4 ounces, which must fit in one clear, quart-size bag — a policy known as the 3-1-1 rule.

The T.S.A. initially banned all liquids in carry-on bags in August 2006 after British intelligence thwarted the terrorist plot. That policy was eventually eased and replaced with the 3-1-1 rule.

Hamed Aleaziz contributed reporting.

Follow New York Times Travel on Instagram and sign up for our Travel Dispatch newsletter to get expert tips on traveling smarter and inspiration for your next vacation. Dreaming up a future getaway or just armchair traveling? Check out our 52 Places to Go in 2026.

item.title: McClatchy Makes Deep Job Cuts to Newspapers Around the Country
item.description:
McClatchy, the newspaper chain that owns The Miami Herald, The Sacramento Bee and 28 other newspapers, made deep job cuts on Thursday to newsrooms across the country.

At The Herald, more than 30 roles were cut — more than a third of the editorial staff — while the newsroom of its sister paper, the Spanish-language El Nuevo Herald, was almost completely eliminated, four people with knowledge of the layoffs said.

At outlets in the Pacific Northwest, including The Bellingham Herald in Washington and The Idaho Statesman in Boise, 17 journalists, about a third of unionized workers, were jettisoned, according to the union, the Pacific Northwest Newspaper Guild. At The Lexington Herald-Leader in Kentucky, the majority of the newsroom was laid off.

The full extent of the cuts was not yet clear, but a current employee who asked to remain anonymous said at least 90 journalists had been laid off at dozens of publications.

Carol Marbin Miller, the deputy investigations editor of The Herald, said in an interview that the layoffs and elimination of vacant positions were “a blood bath.”

“We’re all gobsmacked by the breadth of the cuts,” she said. “I have seen multiple rounds of layoffs or buyouts. I cannot remember a day in which 30 slots were wiped off the slate.”

Greg Farmer, the chain’s executive vice president of local news, was blunt in an email to McClatchy newsrooms on Thursday afternoon. “We cannot continue investing where subscriber interest does not support the investment,” he wrote.

He said McClatchy had maintained its level of investment in local news for the past five years, but that consumer revenue during that time had dropped 41 percent while expenses had stayed flat, requiring “a different choice.” McClatchy will instead invest in journalism that “is differentiated, consequential and difficult to replicate; reporting rooted in our communities and strengthened by sources, investigation, verification, context and judgment,” he said in the email, a copy of which was obtained by The New York Times.

He added that McClatchy remained “deeply committed” to local journalism.

A McClatchy spokeswoman did not respond to requests for comment.

Almost 40 percent of local newspapers in America have shut down in the past two decades, according to a 2025 Northwestern University report on the state of local news, leaving a growing number of areas around the country with little or no local news coverage. Persistent cuts have hollowed out many of the newsrooms that still exist.

McClatchy has newspapers in 14 states and Washington, D.C. Formerly a family-run business, it was sold to the hedge fund Chatham Asset Management in 2020 after it declared bankruptcy.

The company has gone through rounds of layoffs in recent years. In late 2025, McClatchy closed its breaking-news desk and shut down its Washington, D.C., bureau, while carrying out further layoffs across its newspapers.

This year, journalists in many of McClatchy’s newsrooms went public with their intention to withhold their bylines from a new artificial intelligence tool that the company rolled out. The A.I. summarizes articles and produces new versions for different audiences, and the journalists expressed alarm about the company’s use of A.I. content in newspapers.

A person close to the executive decision-making, who asked to remain anonymous, told The Times that the layoffs were not related to the use of A.I. and instead were about business performance in some areas.

Ms. Marbin Miller, who has worked at The Herald for 26 years and was not laid off on Thursday, said management had told Herald journalists in recent meetings that they were not productive enough and had to focus on “generating more page views, more engagement.”

She said the cuts, which included the paper’s City Hall reporter, left her with real concern about the future of journalism in Miami.

“Miami is about to become a news desert,” Ms. Marbin Miller said. “Even if we survive these cuts, there just won’t be enough of us left to do a fraction of what this market requires.”
